title: The Evil Culture Of Online Teaching
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin names a specific pressure he sees consuming online teachers: a culture of perfectionism, competition, and technological one-upmanship that formed out of last spring's distance-learning criticisms, endless summer trainings, and administrative pressure. He argues this culture is an illusion that can be broken by holding onto three truths: that highly polished, tech-heavy lessons are actually boring for students; that simplicity focused on a single objective wins over flashy production; and that genuine human connection, not slick video, is what actually motivates and teaches students. His closing call is for teachers to consciously 'zag' against colleagues chasing technological perfection, arguing that returning to simple, connected, well-taught lessons is both easier on teachers and more effective for students.
points: A culture of perfectionism and tech competition, not any single tool or administrator, is what's driving teacher burnout online.
Highly produced, technology-heavy lessons are often less effective and more boring than simple, direct instruction.
Focus each online lesson on one objective and prove understanding, rather than layering in unnecessary tools.
Genuine human connection through the camera, not slick production value, is what actually motivates students to learn.
Deliberately resist peer pressure to match colleagues' technological showmanship — simplicity is not a lesser standard.
quotes: It’s a culture, you see, of perfection, competition, and long hours toiling away at your desk.
It’s a culture that boxes you in and forces you to be someone you’re not and never wanted to be.
Your students don’t need you to compete with TicTok, video games, or their favorite YouTube channels (nor can you). They just need you to be YOU and share your passion for your subject.
But nothing is going to be as effective as you, standing in front of the camera with your wits, humor, and personality.
It is you, and only you, that can build influential, behavior-changing, intrinsically motivating rapport.
So I encourage you, when your colleagues are zigging, zag to your heart’s content.
